title: A Lament for Pharaoh and the Nations in the Pit
summary: Ezekiel raises a funeral lament over Pharaoh, pictured as a sea monster that God hauls out in his net and leaves on the land, while the heavens go dark over Egypt. The sword of the king of Babylon will break Egypt's pride. In a second oracle the prophet escorts Egypt down to the underworld, where the fallen empires of the past, Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, and the Sidonians, lie in disgrace among the uncircumcised.
story: This is the last of Ezekiel's oracles against the nations, and it closes the section that began in chapter 25. The great powers that surrounded Judah, and on which Judah had leaned or against which it had struggled, are all brought low. The dates show that these words come after news of Jerusalem's fall had reached the exiles (33:21 records that report in the tenth month of the twelfth year). With the city gone, the question was whether any power on earth was stronger than the God of Israel. The answer of chapter 32 is that every empire ends in the same pit. With the nations dealt with, the book turns in chapter 33 to the prophet's renewed commission and to restoration.
historical:
The first oracle is dated to the first day of the twelfth month of the twelfth year, about March 585 BC; the second, to the fifteenth day of a month that the Hebrew doesn't name (the Greek translation supplies the first month), probably a little earlier or later in the same year. Pharaoh Hophra (Apries) still ruled Egypt. Verse 11 names the agent plainly: "The sword of the king of Babylon will come against you", that is, Nebuchadnezzar II.

The nations in the underworld were real powers from Israel's recent memory. Assyria had fallen in the late seventh century BC. Elam, a kingdom east of Babylonia centered on Susa, was devastated by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in the middle of that century. Meshech and Tubal were peoples of central and eastern Anatolia (modern Turkey) known from Assyrian records, remembered as fierce warriors. Edom was Judah's neighbor to the southeast, and the Sidonians were the Phoenicians of the coast. Each had spread terror in its day; each now lies among the slain.
cultural:
The "monster in the seas" of verse 2 translates tannin, a word used for large sea or river creatures and sometimes for the chaos dragon of ancient myth. For Egypt it likely suggests the Nile crocodile, a creature connected in Egyptian religion with royal and divine power. The picture of God throwing a net over the monster echoes older Near Eastern stories in which a god captures a chaos beast; here the monster is only a king, and Israel's God catches him with ease. The darkening of sun, moon, and stars (verses 7 to 8) would strike hard in Egypt, where the sun god Ra was central to royal ideology.

The second oracle draws on beliefs about burial. A proper grave with one's weapons and honors mattered deeply. The mighty warriors of old in verse 27 go down to Sheol with their swords under their heads and shields on their bones, a picture of honorable burial. The nations of this chapter do not share that honor; they lie among the uncircumcised and those slain by the sword, the dishonored dead. The lament (qinah) was a formal funeral song, often chanted by professional women mourners, which is why verse 16 says the daughters of the nations will chant it.
literary: The chapter holds two oracles. The first (verses 1 to 16) is labeled a lament but mostly announces judgment, beginning with the image of Pharaoh as a lion and a sea monster and ending with the promise that the nations will chant this lament. The second (verses 17 to 32) is a tour of the underworld, a kind of roll call of the dead, built with heavy repetition. Nation after nation is introduced ("Assyria is there", "Elam is there", "Meshech and Tubal are there", "Edom is there"), and each entry repeats the same phrases: slain, fallen by the sword, uncircumcised, those who descend to the Pit, who once spread terror in the land of the living. The repetition has the effect of a tolling bell. Pharaoh arrives at the end and finds grim comfort in the company.

outline.t: Date and lament: Pharaoh the lion and sea monster
Caught in God's net, the heavens darkened
The sword of Babylon and the lament of the nations
Egypt sent down to the Pit
The roll call of the fallen nations

doctrines.note: The chapter shows the end of every power that rules by terror. The repeated phrase "who once spread terror in the land of the living" names the charge, and the grave names the verdict. God judges not only Israel but the nations for the violence they did.

God spreads the net, darkens the heavens, and sends the sword of Babylon. Even the terror of verse 32 is his: "I will spread My terror in the land of the living". No empire, however feared, stands outside his rule.
The refrain "then they will know that I am the LORD" (verse 15) states the goal of God's acts in history. Judgment serves the revelation of who God is.

words.note: Qinah, dirge or lament. A funeral song with a recognizable limping rhythm in Hebrew poetry. Ezekiel uses the form ironically: it is a funeral song sung over a king who is still alive, announcing his death in advance.

Chittit, terror. The word appears seven times in the roll call and elsewhere in the Old Testament only once, in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre (26:17). The terror these nations inspired is the very thing that marks them for judgment.

Arel, uncircumcised. Ten times in this chapter. For Egypt, which practiced circumcision, to be counted among the uncircumcised was a mark of shame, and for Israel the word meant those outside the covenant.
Bor, pit. A cistern or well, and by extension the grave and the underworld. Those who descend to the Pit is a stock phrase for the dead.

christ: The link here is thematic. Chapter 32 shows the powers of the world, each once terrifying, lying in the dust together, and it leaves the reader asking whether anything can reach into the Pit. The Old Testament begins to answer in Ezekiel's own later vision of dry bones raised to life (chapter 37). The New Testament proclaims that Christ went into death and came out of it, holding the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18), and that he disarmed the powers and authorities, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). Revelation's great dragon draws on the same family of sea-monster images, and there too the monster is finally overcome. Ezekiel does not predict these things; he shows the need they answer.

hard.q: Does this chapter teach what the afterlife is like?
hard.a: It is better read as poetic taunt than as a map of the afterlife. Ezekiel uses the common Israelite picture of Sheol as a shadowy realm below the earth where the dead lie together, and he arranges the nations in it for rhetorical effect: the honored and the dishonored, the circumcised and the uncircumcised, the graves arranged around each nation. Some interpreters see in the distinction between the honored warriors of verse 27 and the shamed nations an early sign that the Bible's picture of the dead was developing toward distinctions of destiny. Others caution that the distinctions here concern honor in burial and memory, not reward and punishment after death. The fuller hope of resurrection comes later in the Old Testament (Daniel 12:2) and is central in the New. Chapter 32 should not be pressed for details it never set out to give.

questions: Each nation in the roll call once spread terror in the land of the living. What does it tell you about power that its end looks so much the same for everyone?
Pharaoh finds comfort that others have fallen too (verse 31). Why is that a hollow comfort, and where do people seek it today?
The exiles had just lost their city. How might hearing that every empire comes under God's judgment have helped or troubled them?
